title: Advanced relative clauses and prepositions
objectives: Form relative clauses with stranded and fronted prepositions.
Choose whom or which after a fronted preposition.
Distinguish location from direction in relative clauses.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A relative clause can contain a preposition related to its verb or adjective. In ‘the colleague who I spoke to’, to belongs to speak to. The relative word refers to the colleague, and the preposition remains at the end of the clause. This position is common in conversation and informal writing.

A more formal alternative places the preposition before whom or which: ‘the colleague to whom I spoke’ and ‘the proposal about which we spoke’. In these patterns, whom refers to a person and which to a thing. Moving the preposition changes the register, not necessarily the core meaning.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: In a defining clause, an object relative pronoun can often be omitted when the preposition stays at the end: ‘the colleague I spoke to’ and ‘the proposal we discussed’. With a stranded preposition, who, whom or that may refer to a person, and which or that may refer to a thing: ‘the person who/that I spoke to’ and ‘the subject which/that we spoke about’.

When the preposition comes before the relative pronoun, use whom for a person and which for a thing in standard formal English: ‘the colleague to whom I spoke’ and ‘the subject about which we spoke’. Do not place that directly after the preposition in this pattern. In non-defining clauses, commas set off extra information and the relative pronoun is not normally omitted.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare ‘The organisation that she works for supports artists’ with ‘The organisation for which she works supports artists’. The first is common in everyday English. The second is more formal. Both identify an organisation, but the verb pattern work for still determines the preposition for.

Where can replace in which or at which for many place references: ‘the office where I work’ and ‘the office in which I work’. Do not assume where can replace every preposition: ‘the city to which she moved’ expresses direction, while ‘the city where she lived’ expresses location. The meaning of the preposition matters.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use a preposition before that in the formal pattern: ‘the topic about which we spoke’, not ‘the topic about that we spoke’. With that, leave the preposition at the end: ‘the topic that we spoke about’. Do not repeat the relative reference with an extra object: ‘the colleague who I spoke to’, not ‘the colleague who I spoke to her’.

A sentence-final preposition is standard English and is often the natural choice in speech. Fronting the preposition can be appropriate in formal prose but may sound overly formal in everyday conversation. Some phrasal verbs do not lend themselves naturally to fronting: ‘the child she looks after’ is natural; ‘the child after whom she looks’ is awkward for many speakers.

examples.sentence: The colleague who I spoke to called.
examples.note: The preposition is stranded at the end of the defining clause.

examples.sentence: The colleague to whom I spoke called.
examples.note: Fronted to whom is a more formal alternative.

examples.sentence: The topic that we spoke about was useful.
examples.note: That is possible with the preposition at the end.

examples.sentence: The topic about which we spoke was useful.
examples.note: About which is a formal fronted pattern.

examples.sentence: The office where I work is nearby.
The office in which I work is nearby.
examples.note: In which is a more formal location pattern.

examples.sentence: The organisation for which she works supports artists.
examples.note: The verb pattern is work for.

examples.sentence: The child she looks after is asleep.
examples.note: The object relative pronoun is omitted in a natural everyday pattern.

common_errors.incorrect: The topic about that we spoke was useful.
common_errors.correct: The topic about which we spoke was useful.
common_errors.reason: Use which after a fronted preposition in this formal pattern.

common_errors.incorrect: The colleague who I spoke to her called.
common_errors.correct: The colleague who I spoke to called.
common_errors.reason: Do not repeat the relative reference with her.

common_errors.incorrect: The office in where I work is nearby.
common_errors.correct: The office where I work is nearby.
common_errors.reason: Use where or in which for this location pattern.

summary: A preposition may remain at the end of a relative clause or appear before whom or which in a formal pattern.
Do not use that directly after a fronted preposition in standard formal English.
Where can express a place relationship, but the intended preposition and meaning matter.

exercises.prompt: The colleague ___ I spoke called. Choose the formal fronted pattern.
exercises.explanation: Use to whom for a person after the fronted preposition.

option_feedback.b: “to who” does not fit here. Use to whom for a person after the fronted preposition.
option_feedback.c: “to that” does not fit here. Use to whom for a person after the fronted preposition.
option_feedback.d: “to where” does not fit here. Use to whom for a person after the fronted preposition.

option_feedback.d: “about where” does not fit here. Use about which for the thing after the fronted preposition.

option_feedback.c: “who” does not fit here. Where refers to the place of work.

exercises.prompt: The organisation ___ she works supports artists. Use the everyday stranded pattern.

exercises.prompt: The city ___ she moved is far away. Choose the formal expression of direction.
exercises.explanation: To which expresses the direction of the move.

option_feedback.b: “in where” does not fit here. To which expresses the direction of the move.
option_feedback.c: “at whom” does not fit here. To which expresses the direction of the move.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is natural in everyday English?
exercises.explanation: The object pronoun can be omitted and after remains with looks.

The child after she looks whom is asleep.

option_feedback.d: “The child after she looks whom is asleep.” does not fit here. The object pronoun can be omitted and after remains with looks.
